rows: Invasive meningococcal disease is rare but can cause meningitis or sepsis.
Suspected cases require urgent clinical treatment and public-health notification.
Public-health teams assess close contacts and exposure circumstances.
Eligible close contacts may be offered antibiotic chemoprophylaxis.
Vaccination may be recommended for specific cases, clusters or risk groups.
Laboratory confirmation and serogroup information support public-health action.
Symptoms can progress rapidly and may not appear in a fixed order.
Clusters and outbreaks require coordinated investigation, communication and control.
A symptom, school notice or regional case count does not establish meningococcal disease in an individual.
Case and contact decisions require clinical, laboratory, timing, exposure and public-health evidence.
Active tuberculosis is a notifiable disease in England.
Suspected or confirmed active TB should be notified through the required public-health process.
TB can spread through inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets from a person with pulmonary disease.
Diagnosis uses clinical assessment, imaging, microbiology and other relevant tests.
Public-health management can include contact tracing and screening.
Latent TB infection and active TB disease require different assessment and management.
Treatment adherence and drug-susceptibility information are important for control.
UKHSA surveillance supports local and national TB prevention action.
A positive screening test or residence in a high-incidence area does not by itself establish active infectious TB.
Individual conclusions require symptoms, imaging, microbiology, treatment and exposure evidence.
Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox and can later reactivate as shingles.
Chickenpox is highly infectious to susceptible contacts.
Exposure management should consider the infectious period and the contact's immunity.
Pregnant people, immunosuppressed people and newborns can require urgent specialist assessment after exposure.
Post-exposure prophylaxis can include antivirals or immunoglobulin for eligible high-risk contacts.
Timing is important when assessing and delivering post-exposure prophylaxis.
Laboratory testing can be used when confirmation or immunity assessment is required.
Current UKHSA guidance should be followed because recommended products and pathways can change.
A rash or exposure report does not establish chickenpox, shingles or susceptibility.
Management requires clinical features, timing, immunity, pregnancy or immune status and exposure evidence.
Food businesses must provide accurate information about regulated allergens.
Allergen-information requirements depend on whether food is prepacked, prepacked for direct sale or non-prepacked.
Businesses should identify allergen ingredients and manage recipe or supplier changes.
Cross-contact risk should be assessed and controlled through suitable procedures.
Staff need training to provide reliable allergen information.
Written information and a conversation with customers can support safer service in the out-of-home sector.
Precautionary allergen labelling should follow a risk-based approach rather than replace good controls.
Allergen incidents and near misses should prompt investigation and corrective action.
An allergen-free claim or menu statement does not prove absence of cross-contact in a specific serving.
Serving-level conclusions require recipe, supplier, preparation, cleaning, communication and cross-contact evidence.
